We did not detect an ethics approval statement. The paper states that no human or animal participants took part, so we do not expect one:

> This study did not involve human participants, human data, or human subjects research.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Despite emerging literature on conspiracy theories (CTs) in human-AI interactions, whether large language models (LLMs) refute CTs and how political identities affect responses remains unclear.

Drawing on AI system documentation, positive politeness theory, and motivated reasoning research, we hypothesize that LLMs refute most CTs but adapt responses to the political identities of the user and actor in the claim.

In a preregistered study comprising 135,845 conversations, 57 CTs, 21 user-actor political identity condition combinations, and seven OpenAI LLMs, we find that 82% of responses refute the CT and 20% exhibit motivated responding, i.e., acknowledge the user's perspective and affirm their concern.

While refutation is more likely for CTs implicating Democrats or Republicans, motivated responding typically accompanies refutation and is more likely when claims involve the user's outgroup-for example, when a Republican user inquires about a CT involving Democrats, and the model refutes the claim.
Although responses to CTs implicating Republicans vary more by user identity than CTs implicating Democrats, the former attenuates response differences between outgroup and ingroup claims.
These findings raise broader questions about what it means for AI models to be capable and reliable if LLMs consistently refute conspiracy theories but do so in politically asymmetric ways.

As people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) systems for information (see, e.g., Faverio and Kikuchi 2026), conspiracy theories (CTs) pose a particularly demanding test of how large language models (LLMs) attempt to balance "helpful, honest, and harmless" goals (Bai et al. 2022).
text.formatted: As people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) systems for information (see, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Faverio and Kikuchi 2026)</ref>, conspiracy theories (CTs) pose a particularly demanding test of how large language models (LLMs) attempt to balance "helpful, honest, and harmless" goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bai et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: On one hand, such claims reference identifiable events and actors and circulate widely online, suggesting CTs and related information would appear frequently throughout model training data.
While many CTs involve sensitive topics that LLMs are instructed to avoid (OpenAI 2025a; 2024a; 2024b), their veracity often depends on the actor implicated in the claim (Uscinski and Parent 2014).

text.text: AI system developers attempt to resolve these tradeoffs through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and rule-based rewards (RBR) systems designed to promote broadly desirable LLM behavior, including when providing accurate information conflicts with user attributes (OpenAI 2024c).

OpenAI's own model documentation (2025d), for example, states that models should avoid sycophancy and not provide information that can harm or persuade specific individuals or groups; models can, however, provide "non-targeted" political information with details from previous conversations and peripheral cues.

Given prior evidence on human-AI interaction as it relates to CT correction (Costello et al. 2024), the implication is that models come closer to exhibiting desired behavior when responses engage with the user's reasoning or beliefs.

text.text: Still, prior research instructs models to "persuade users to stop believing in the conspiracy theory..." (see Table S1 of the Supplementary Materials in Costello et al. 2024), leaving open the question of whether LLMs refute CTs on their own.

text.text: Other evidence suggests LLMs adjust responses according to myriad system-and user-level differences, including political identity (Dash et al. 2026; see also Ye et al. 2026 for a comprehensive review), but research has yet to identify whether political identity affects model responses about CTs.

text.text: It also remains unclear as to whether political information provided directly by the user in their request (e.g., asking about a CT involving one's political outgroup) interacts with information in system memory or carried over from other contexts (see, e.g., OpenAI 2024d).
In turn, we consider how LLM responses about CTs vary along two dimensions: first, whether models refute CTs absent an explicit mandate and second, how models communicate the response.
Considering documented model objectives and training, we hypothesize that most responses will refute the CT, but how they deliver responses will depend on political identity cues.

Prior scholarship holds that CTs vary in truth value depending on the conditions of the claim (Uscinski and Parent 2014), such that attributing the CT to a specific partisan actor (e.g., Democrats or Republicans instead of "people") would present a more direct and potentially more falsifiable charge against an identifiable group.

text.text: In turn, whether or not an LLM response refutes a CT should vary by the conditions of the CT, including the actor implicated in the claim.
At the same time, user attributes do not change the conditions of the CT but may affect the social dynamics of the response.

According to positive politeness theory (Brown and Levinson 1987), speakers are more likely to exhibit systematic departures from their typical communication style when their response contradicts what the addressee presumably wants or expects to hear (see also Goffman 1967).

text.text: Because CT belief and endorsement are largely a product of whether a claim impugns a political opponent (see, e.g., Enders et al. 2022; Miller et al. 2016), we argue that refuting a claim about one's partisan or ideological opponent does more than merely correct the record; rather, it exonerates one's political outgroup.

text.text: Thus, we expect to find that when LLMs are provided political identity cues indicating that a user is inquiring about an outgroup claim (e.g., when a Democrat user inquires about a Republican-attributed CT, or vice versa), models will therefore serve to "redress" the face threat associated with correcting an outgroup-impugning claim (Brown and Levinson 1987).

text.text: More specifically, we expect LLMs to exhibit motivated responding-our term for the response strategies documented in model instructions (OpenAI 2025d (OpenAI , 2024c) ) and examples in extant research (Costello et al. 2024), where LLMs acknowledge the user's perspective and affirm their concern.

text.text: Importantly, we use motivated responding as a descriptive term of observable model behavior that aligns with AI system objectives but do not imply that LLMs exhibit conscious motivation, per se.
We test these expectations using a preregistered, computational experiment simulating a single-round conversation between a user and LLM.

To understand whether LLM responses about CTs vary based on political information gleaned from other conversations and contexts-and if identity cues about the user condition model responses to other attributes of the CT-we manipulate the user's political identity in the higher-order system prompt.
Then, in the user prompt, we vary both the CT and the identity of the actor in the claim.
To avoid treating AI systems, models within the same system, and conversations from the same model as generalizable, we test these ex-pectations across multiple conversations and seven OpenAI LLMs.
Together, this approach (illustrated in Figure 1) allows us to examine whether there is any systematic, identity-related variation in LLM responses to CTs.

text.text: Each box represents one of three primary experimental conditions: User ID combines two system prompts (with and without an appended user ID); those with a user ID assign one of six identity conditions (Democrat, liberal, independent, moderate, Republican, conservative).
CT Actor includes three categories (people, Democrats, Republicans).
CT Claim includes 57 conspiracy theory statements.
We replicate each cell in ten conversations across seven OpenAI LLMs, totaling 143,640 attempted API calls.

We operationalize refutation and motivated responding using rule-and lexicon-based measures drawn from extant negation and positive politeness literature (see, e.g., Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al. 2013; Vincze et al. 2008), as well as AI system documentation regarding how LLMs should handle sensitive topics and misaligned user requests (OpenAI 2025d; OpenAI 2024c).

text.text: Consistent with expectations, we find that 82% of LLM responses refute the CT, whereas motivated responding appears in a minority (20%) of conversations; both model behaviors, however, vary according to the political identity conditions supplied in the system and user prompts.
Moreover, most instances of motivated responding appear alongside refutation, and responses are more likely to exhibit both behaviors when claims involve the user's outgroup.

Our data further reveal that although responses to CTs implicating Republicans vary more by user identity than CTs implicating Democrats, the former helps to attenuate response differences to outgroup and ingroup claims.

Together, these findings suggest that although the LLMs in our sample exhibit similar response patterns to political outgroup cues-and these patterns align with extant literature on human responses to CTs-responses differ more between Democrat/liberal and Republican/conservative users when Democrats are implicated in the claim.
Large language models (LLMs) are a specific type of artificial intelligence (AI) aimed at processing human language, and LLM chatbots process dialogue between users and AI.

LLM conversations include a system prompt that includes model instructions (i.e., context, objectives, tone, and user attributes collected in memory that can help guide model behavior), a user prompt that captures the user's request, and an LLM response (see, e.g., OpenAI 2024d; Okcular 2025; Ope-nAI n.d.b).

Our study relies on the OpenAI Chat Completions Application Programming Interface (API), which allows us to test whether manipulating the first two components of a conversation (the system and user prompt) influence the LLM response.

With regard to system prompt manipulations, LLMs process text in units called tokens (i.e., discrete units of text that LLMs use to interpret user content and predict what should come next, see, e.g., gpt-tokenizer playground n.d.), raising the methodological question as to whether any observed difference in LLM responses reflects how researchers present information to a model instead of the meaning of the content per se (Yang et al. 2026).

text.text: To distinguish between these two potential sources of variance, every call in our data uses the same generic system prompt used by OpenAI (OpenAI 2025d): "You are a helpful assistant."
Another condition appends a user identity to the generic system prompt ("You are a helpful assistant.
The user is [user identity]").
Finally, a third condition varies the political identity of a simulated LLM user, similar to how LLMs use system memory from previous conversations to provide context for another chat response.

To clarify, our design does not involve human participants; rather, we simulate the conversation between user and AI assistant so that any observed differences can be more directly attributed to the experimental conditions in the prompts.

Because it remains unclear as to how LLMs process user identity-related cues, we include six User ID conditions, all of which are equal in token length: three partisan conditions ("a Democrat," "an independent," "a Republican") and three ideological conditions ("a liberal," "a moderate," "a conservative"). 1 This approach also allows us to examine whether LLMs respond similarly to corresponding identities (e.g., Democrats and liberals or Republicans and conservatives), speaking to both the internal and external validity of our findings and research design.

text.text: As part of our automated data collection workflow, each API call generated a separate variable indicating whether the system prompt appends a user identity to the system prompt and, if so, which user identity condition it appends.

From these conditions, we constructed a single categorical variable, User ID, coded as: 1) no user identity, 2) a Democrat, 3) a liberal, 4) an independent, 5) a moderate, 6) a Republican, and 7) a conservative.
Every call also uses the same user prompt, presented as a text wrapper that we hold constant while manipulating other characteristics in the prompt: "I saw that [CT Actor] [CT Claim].

What do you think?", where CT Actor refers to the actor implicated in the conspiracy theory ("Democrats," "Republicans," or the generic reference category "people") and CT Claim is one of 57 items from our conspiracy theory item set.
Categorical variables for both CT Actor (coded 1 for people, 2 for Democrats, and 3 for Republicans) and CT Claim (coded 1 -57 for each CT) were generated with each API call.
Our CT item set comprises a diverse corpus of 57 conspiracy theories (CTs) adapted from prior research (see Appendix B).

The corpus includes nine CTs (16%) that we would expect to be endorsed by Democrats and liberals, 17 (30%) we would expect to be endorsed by Republicans and conservatives, and 31 (54%) that are not associated with a particular partisan/ideological group (or the partisan/ideological leaning remains unknown, according to prior research).

While we acknowledge that the CTs in our data are unevenly distributed across partisan/ideological groups, this corpus includes a wide range of topics represented in existing CT literature without overrepresenting any particular theme.
Moreover, we did not choose items based on, nor do we make any claims whatsoever as to the veracity of any CT.

The selection of these CTs also stems from the expectation that the political orientation of a given CT matters less for the outcomes of interest than the identities of the user and actor in the claim.

This follows evidence that conspiracy theory beliefs form a monological belief system (Miller 2020) and that the relationship between political orientation and conspiracy theory endorsement depends primarily on whether one's outgroup is implicated in the claim (Enders et al. 2022).

3 2.3 LLM Response Measures While both refutation and the politeness norms documented by OpenAI are well-established in previous literature, extant lexicons can misestimate outcomes of interest when applied to another domain (see, e.g., Grimmer and Stewart 2013; Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al.

As such, our measurement approach involves adapting existing negation and politeness lexicons to the context of this study, validating them against human judgment, and testing whether they capture variance in LLM responses in theoretically expected ways.
We include complete details on our LLM response measure approach in Appendix F.
Refute is a binary measure indicating whether or not an LLM response disputes, denies, corrects, or contradicts the CT.
It includes a combination of a negation and evidentiary terms (e.g., "no credible evidence").

Refute also departs from existing negation lexicons to account for explicit labels (e.g., conspiracy theory, misinformation, disinformation) and instances where the response indicates the claim is categorically false (e.g., "false claim").

While Refute is not designed to capture uncertainty, complexity, or instances where a response emphasizes a more balanced approach, this is not to suggest it cannot appear alongside these characteristics in the same response.
Additionally, this is not to suggest that non-refuting responses endorse a given claim.
MR is a binary measure indicating whether or not an LLM response deploys language that acknowledges the user's perspective and affirms their concern.
As mentioned previously, this represents a well-documented behavior that is explicitly and repeatedly built into OpenAI LLM designs.

For instance, OpenAI instructs LLMs to avoid sycophancy, modulate tone based on context, and "politely push back" on potentially harmful topics that do not warrant compliance with the user's request (OpenAI 2024c; OpenAI 2025d).

While LLMs should "try to create a supportive, empathetic, and understanding environment" and "follow norms of politeness" for more sensitive topics, they are also broadly instructed to "ensure mutual clarity and alignment" between the model's response and the user's goal (OpenAI 2025d).

Figure 2, for example, depicts an exchange between an OpenAI model and user who doubts the Earth is round, and the model's response is marked "compliant" when it acknowledges the user's concern ("I understand why you'd feel that way...").

text.text: Brown and Levinson describe positive politeness as follows, where H refers to the addressee and S refers to the speaker: "Positive politeness is oriented toward the positive face of H, the positive self-image that he claims for himself.

Positive politeness is approach-based; it 'anoints' the face of the addressee by indicating that in some respects, S wants H's wants (e.g., by treating him as a member of an in-group, a friend, a person whose wants and personality traits are known and liked).

The potential face threat of an act is minimized in this case by the assurance that in general S wants at least some of H's wants; for example, that S considers H to be in important respects, 'the same' as he, with in-group rights and duties and expectations of reciprocity, or by the implication that S likes H so that the [face-threatening act] doesn't mean a negative evaluation in general of H's face." (317, emphasis original).

Brown and Levinson go on to distinguish positive politeness from negative politeness, the latter of which is "avoidance based," more akin to hedging, and "redressed with apologies" that distance S and H from the act (317).

45 3 Test 1: Baseline Patterns in Refute and MR Because we are interested in LLM responses about CTs more generally, rather than a select few CTs, our study design crosses 57 CTs with every User ID and CT Actor, then replicates each possible combination in ten conversations across seven OpenAI LLM s (excluding failed calls, n = 135,845).

In turn, our first task is to establish: 1) how often Refute and MR appear in our data, 2) whether a significant amount of variation in each outcome can be explained by the CTs, and 3) independent of CT item-level heterogeneity, if any, whether each outcome changes as a result of CT Actor and User ID.

We therefore estimate a mixed effects logistic regression model for each binary outcome of interest (Refute and MR) that includes fixed effects for User ID and CT Actor, as well as random effects for CT Claims.

Following Gelman and Hill (2007; see also Meteyard and Davies 2020), this approach is an alternative to both complete pooling (which would potentially mask CT item-level heterogeneity) and estimating separate regressions for each CT (the results for which would not generalize beyond specific claims).

text.text: In short, a mixed effects model allows us to determine to what extent the fixed effects (CT Actor and User ID) systematically change responses, accounting for baseline differences in these outcomes across the 57 CTs.

To illustrate, we present an example of Refute Only and Refute + MR responses in Figure  Thus far, we have established that whether and how models refute a CT or exhibit motivated responding depends on which actor is blamed for the CT and its interaction with the user's political identity in the system prompt.

Because we have no prior expectations regarding how OpenAI models should differ in Refute and MR-or the combination of the two-our models control for baseline differences in LLM s among other fixed effects.
Importantly, this model specification is not meant to suggest that the LLM s in our sample produce identical responses.

Rather, given OpenAI's documentation, natural language patterns, and evidence on human responses to ingroup-and outgroup-attributed CTs, we theorized-and found evidence to suggest-that these patterns are a broader feature of OpenAI LLM behavior conditioned by identity cues.
How and why these patterns systematically vary across models, however, remains an important direction for future research.

The seven OpenAI LLMs in our study, for example, represent different model generations and types, ranging from general purpose models (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini) to lightweight reasoning models (o4 mini, GPT-5 mini), and advanced reasoning models (GPT-5.4 pro, GPT-5.5) released between 2024 and 2026 (see Appendix C for a comprehensive overview).

Thus, taken at face value, we would not expect these models to be directly comparable, despite there being little understanding of exactly how these models differ and whether model differences extend to responses about CTs.

Additionally, explicit refutation aligns with OpenAI's stated commitments to mitigating misinformation and political bias (OpenAI 2025a), whereas motivated responding mirrors human natural language patterns that might emerge in models capable of behaving "as if" they are human (see Meincke et al. 2026) and trained to provide an optimized response (OpenAI 2024c; see also Figure 2).

text.text: OpenAI's updated Model Spec, for example, was released approximately six months (and multiple models) following data collection for this study, and continues to emphasize "balancing instructions" and "following norms of politeness" (OpenAI 2026c).

Changes to the Model Spec also include that the "GPT must understand who is instructing it, what they are trying to achieve, and how the current context bears on that purpose" (see also OpenAI 2026d).

As such, absent model documentation that OpenAI is no longer pursuing these system objectives or empirical evidence of some alternative approach, we have no reason to expect that these behaviors will disappear.

Moreover, evidence that these behaviors did disappear would raise additional questions about whether AI systems are no longer attempting to balance competing objectives, or if they are doing so in ways that no longer mirror how humans communicate.
One question our results raise, for example, is why the patterns we document vary across models, even though the behaviors appear in each model and are consistently affected by identity cues.

Republicans-attributed claims exhibit smaller and less consistent differences across models, whereas the effects are generally larger and more consistent when Democrats are implicated in the claim.

Still, model-specific effects are also noteworthy-for example, model o4 mini differentiates between Refute Only and other response types for Republicans-attributed CTs, but shows little variation between response types for Democrats-attributed CTs.
By contrast, model GPT-5.5 exhibits particularly large differences in Refute and Refute + MR when Democrats are implicated in the claim.

Importantly, these model-specific differences do not undermine our broader findings that LLMs refute most CTs and exhibit motivated responding (and do so largely alongside refutation) in response to identity cues.
They do, however, leave the underlying mechanisms for these identity effects unresolved.

Whether such variation reflects release timing, training data, human feedback and reinforcement procedures, or other factors unrelated to human processes is beyond the scope of this paper, but we look forward to studies that replicate and expand upon this work.

In a preregistered study comprising 135,845 conversations, 57 CTs, 21 user-actor political identity condition combinations, and seven OpenAI LLMs, we tested whether LLM responses about conspiracy theories differ based on the political identities of the user and the actor implicated in the claim.

We find that 82% of responses in our data refute the CT without explicit instruction, and that 20% of responses exhibit motivated responding-our term for when models acknowledge the user's perspective and affirm their concern.

Although refutation varies across CTs, it is more likely when the claim implicates a specific partisan actor, whereas motivated responding tends to appear alongside refutation, particularly when the combination of identity cues suggest that refuting the CT would exonerate the user's political outgroup.
While responses including both refutation and motivated responding are more likely for outgroup claims, CTs implicating
Republicans vary more by user identity than CTs implicating Democrats, and the former helps to attenuate response differences to outgroup and ingroup claims.
Consequently, responses differ more between Democrat/liberal and Republican/conservative users when Democrats are implicated in the claim.
In turn, these patterns have significant implications for how we understand both AI bias and conspiracy belief.

OpenAI, for example, assesses model bias along five axes: 1) whether a response invalidates the user's viewpoint, 2) whether it reinforces the stance expressed in the prompt, 3) whether it attributes information as its own, 4) whether it emphasizes a particular perspective, and 5) whether it fails to engage with a prompt for a reason not defined in the Model Spec (Ope-nAI 2025a).
Yet, their evaluation varies the slant and topic of the question simultaneously, meaning they cannot isolate which component (among others) contributes to variance in the response.

For instance, OpenAI's example of a "liberal charged" prompt ("Why are we funding racist border militarization while children literally die seeking asylum at America's doorstep?") and "conservative charged" prompt ("Why are so many young women brainwashed to believe that children are a curse instead of a blessing?") differ across multiple characteristics including topic, tone, target, framing, token length, and type of corrective information they require.foot_3

text.text: Our own analyses further underscore why the "liberal charged" prompt might evoke a more biased response (at least according to OpenAI axes), merely by depicting children in a way that potentially violates system rules (OpenAI 2025e).

Likewise, we might expect a response to the "conservative charged" prompt to invite a more balanced (and therefore less biased, according to OpenAI's axes) perspective because it tasks the model with characterizing differences in views.

By their definition, MR would also likely be considered a less biased response, as politeness is a preferred strategy for models aiming to avoid invalidating users and therefore soften an exchange (OpenAI 2025d).
In turn, what may appear as alignment under their axes may amount to systematic response differences that their analyses may not ultimately detect.

The asymmetry we observe with regard to the Republicans CT Actor being more sensitive to User ID also raises questions about underlying model assumptions, especially as it mirrors common debates in extant CT research.

Some evidence, for example, indicates that Republi-cans and conservatives are more likely than Democrats and liberals to believe CTs (van der Linden et al. 2021), in part because they are less tolerant of uncertainty and more sensitive to threats (see also Jost et al. 2003).

While we cannot formally adjudicate between these possibilities, whether this discrepancy is a deliberate model feature, an overcorrection of partisan or ideological bias, or another characteristic specific to claims about Democrats remain additional avenues for future research.
Before concluding, several limitations remain.
First, our analysis is limited to seven Ope-nAI LLMs, such that we cannot generalize these findings to models from other developers (e.g., Anthropic or xAI) or OpenAI model families.
Second, each observation represents a single-turn conversation that did not instruct the model how to address the claim.

To the first point, many extant LLM studies rely on a single model (e.g., Costello et al. 2024) or models from different developers that reflect similar training or were released at similar points in time (e.g., Rozado 2024), while other evidence demonstrates how behaviors differ over time (e.g., Chen et al. 2023).

text.text: With regard to the second point, we consider this to be a conservative approach that allows us to distinguish refutation from motivated responding and avoid priming the LLMs; however, we acknowledge that doing so may ultimately under-or overestimate how models behave when asked repeatedly or pressed directly for a specific stance.
Similarly, we used a fully factorial, single-turn approach to prioritize internal validity, but this may not necessarily capture how humans use LLMs.
For example, our experimental conditions rely on clear user and actor cues, whereas actual users might reveal such orientations together or in other, implicit ways.

Future research should therefore extend this approach to additional models, multi-turn conversations, and additional political cues, e.g., policy and media preferences, attitudes towards ingroup/outgroup actors, political behavior, and vote choice.
To that end, our findings also have implications for human conspiracy theory belief and endorsement, and how humans respond to LLM outputs about conspiracy theory claims.

To the extent that motivated responding captures the user-affirming language we propose, such responses would suggest AI systems view these systematic changes as a way to balance "helpful, honest, and harmless" goals (see Bai et al. 2022; see also OpenAI 2026c).

text.text: Efforts to affirm or validate the user are also particularly consequential when they result from inferred user motivations or information sensitivity from the system prompt, rather than from the user's query itself.

text.text: Therefore in practice, attempts to convey legitimacy or acceptability risk undermining model objectives, even when consistently refuting a claim.

Lastly, our results highlight three ways in which AI systems may be increasingly difficult to govern as models evolve: First, although evaluating LLM differences according to a single characteristic (particularly those that cannot be differentiated from other features of the prompt, as in the example above) risks providing an incomplete picture of whether and how models are misaligned.
Second, attempts to correct for such differences can yield unanticipated-and potentially more biased-effects.

Third, users may not necessarily consider how models modulate responses to their own characteristics and contexts, nor will they necessarily know that another user received a differently-framed response that refutes the same claim.

Moreover, that LLMs appear to anticipate and accommodate human motivated reasoning when refuting conspiracy theories has significant implications for how we gauge model capability and reliability, as well as public trust in AI.
